Common psychiatric disorders are highly heritable and polygenic, yet much of their genetic contribution remains unexplained. We sought to improve discovery of additional risk loci and genes by leveraging information from genetically correlated traits and biological annotations.
We presented an analytic framework to improve statistical power for detecting susceptibility genes/variants based on false discovery rate regression (FDR

), which models the prior probability of association as a function of external covariates. The method was applied to six psychiatric disorders/traits. Covariates included summary-statistic signals from 42 genetically correlated traits and 21 gene-level biological annotations. We evaluated performance through simulations, temporal (internal) validation using later, larger GWAS, drug-cluster enrichment analysis, and
functional follow-up of two autism genes using

Temporal validation confirmed that FDRreg applied to smaller samples successfully identified genes that were only later confirmed in larger, higher-powered studies. Drug-cluster enrichment was strengthened for psychiatric medication classes after FDRreg prioritization. Finally, the
IUE experiments showed that two ASD genes identified by the proposed framework play functional roles in embryonic brain development.

By integrating genetically correlated traits and biological annotations, the FDRreg strategy enables the identification of a greater number of significant genes and risk loci. Moreover, the newly associated genes exhibit meaningful biological functions and clinical relevance, offering a valuable approach for uncovering the genetic basis of psychiatric disorders.

Meta-analysis integrated data from related traits using summary statistics, and methods include Fisher’s combined p-values, fixed/random-effects models, and other approaches based on linear combinations of univariate test statistics
. While effective for identifying more loci, these methods risk inflated type I errors if there are correlated phenotypes or overlapping samples
, and struggle with sample heterogeneity or opposing variant effects
. Recent innovations like cross-phenotype association (CPASSOC) and multi-trait analysis of GWAS (MTAG) address some of these issues above, yet limitations remain
. While MTAG efficiently generates trait-specific SNP effect estimates across multiple traits, its computation time for maximum FDR increases exponentially with more traits, limiting its use
. MTAG also assumes a shared variance-covariance matrix of effect sizes for all SNPs, which can inflate false positives when SNPs are null for one trait but not another
. CPASSOC, while useful for meta-analysis, primarily identifies variants associated with at least one trait
, but not effect size estimates for a primary trait of interest.
An alternative paradigm leverages auxiliary covariates in multiple-testing frameworks to prioritize hypotheses

. These covariates can include GWAS data of related phenotypes or external biological evidence (e.g., from experiments or databases). . Despite promise, these methods have seen very limited applications in genetic epidemiology. Relatedly, condFDR computes a ‘conditional’ FDR, given the p-value of a second trait is lower than a certain threshold
and has been used in psychiatry
, but typically deals with only one covariate.

Our FDRreg-based framework offers several key advantages: (1) It outputs test statistics for the primary trait of interest, unlike meta-analysis, which combines evidence across all traits. For instance, it can evaluate SNP significance for schizophrenia (SCZ) while leveraging GWAS data from bipolar disorder and depression, without aggregating associations as meta-analysis does. (2) It avoids MTAG’s restrictive assumptions, such as a shared variance-covariance matrix across traits. (3) FDRreg handles heterogeneous GWAS results adaptively, estimating prior association probabilities and limiting impact from irrelevant traits. (4) It is computationally fast and scalable to large GWAS or omics datasets. (5) It integrates GWAS results from related traits and biological annotations simultaneously, unlike meta-analysis or MTAG. (6) It reveals which biological features drive significant associations, yielding mechanistic insights beyond statistical discovery.

We applied this framework to six psychiatric disorders/traits: major depressive disorder (MDD), schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BPD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and suicide attempt (SA). A note on two false discovery rate measures
Our primary inferential target was the conventional, cumulative (or tail-area) FDR within each SNP, MAGMA, or TWAS analysis. Hypotheses were ranked by estimated local fdr, and tail-area FDR was
calculated as the mean local fdr among selected hypotheses. The procedure was not intended to guarantee separate FDR control within every covariate stratum.

the FDRreg framework is able to estimate both the local false discovery rate (lfdr) and the conventional (tail-area) false discovery rate (FDR) leveraging external covariate information. The lfdr is a

metric, representing the posterior probability that a particular finding is null given its observed test statistic and covariate profile. In contrast, the cumulative FDR is the expected proportion of false positives among all discoveries that are at least as extreme as a given significance threshold. When hypotheses are ranked by local fdr, the cumulative FDR up to rank
can be derived by the average local fdr among the top

hypotheses. Given that the cumulative FDR is a more well-established and widely used approach for reporting significance in biological and genomic studies, we focused on this metric for our primary results. We conducted three types of validatio

To empirically test whether the FDRreg framework preferentially identifies true disease susceptibility genes, we performed an internal validation analysis. The core objective was to determine if FDRreg, when applied to an earlier, smaller GWAS, could more accurately predict the significant genes later confirmed by a larger, higher-powered GWAS of the same disorder
compared with a standard Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) FDR analysis of the earlier GWAS

As later consortium releases could include samples from earlier GWAS, the temporal validation is best interpreted as prospective prioritization rather than a fully independent replication.

The present study demonstrates that integrating genetically correlated traits and biological annotations through FDR regression (FDRreg) substantially enhances the discovery of genetic associations across psychiatric disorders. By applying this framework to six psychiatric conditions, we identified hundreds of additional significant genes and risk loci that would have been missed by conventional analyses.
Our FDRreg framework offers several key advantages over existing approaches. First, unlike meta-analysis methods that aggregate evidence across traits, FDRreg outputs
statistics while borrowing strength from auxiliary information.
Second, FDRreg avoids the restrictive assumptions of MTAG, such as requiring a shared variance-covariance matrix across traits, and scales efficiently to handle

a large number of auxiliary covariates. Third, condFDR is conceptually close to our framework, but is typically applied with one auxiliary phenotype at a time, making it less straightforward for our setting with multiple GWAS-derived covariates. Importantly, neither MTAG nor condFDR was designed to handle biological annotations or functional

Genetic-correlation and heritability-enrichment analyses also provide information regarding shared genetic basis across disorders and the importance of functional annotations. On the other hand, FDRreg is discovery-oriented and complements, rather than replaces, these approaches. Genetic correlation summarizes genome-wide sharing between pairs of traits, whereas stratified LDSC and SumHer quantify annotation-level heritability enrichment. In contrast, FDRreg translates hypothesis-level auxiliary evidence into a covariate-dependent prior probability of association, providing both increased power for target-trait discovery and interpretable estimates of which covariates contribute most to prioritization.

More broadly, other existing cross-phenotype methods address related but distinct objectives. For example, CPASSOC targets variants associated with at least one of the analyzed traits under a meta-analysis framework, but does not produce trait-specific results.

Taken together, all the above-mentioned approaches have goals that differ from our setting, which aims to integrate multiple GWAS-derived covariates and biological annotations simultaneously to improve discovery for a prespecified target phenotype.
Simulation support, efficiency gains, and tier-specific discovery patterns

The robustness of our approach was rigorously validated through comprehensive simulations demonstrating proper FDR control even with high-dimensional covariates (with potentially only few informative covariates). FDRreg adaptively weights covariates and scales efficiently to large datasets. Crucially, we also showed for the first time that pre-analysis variable selection

LASSO, elastic net, or MA test maintains FDR control, while achieving 8-20 fold computational speed improvements. This innovation enables practical application to large-scale genomic datasets with hundreds of potential covariates.

In our real-data applications, discovery gains were notably larger at the MAGMA and TWAS tiers than at the SNP level. This aligns with the biological nature of psychiatric pleiotropy, which converges more consistently at the level of genes, expression profiles, and pathways. Because of allelic heterogeneity, different individual variants within the same gene can influence related disorders. Consequently, auxiliary gene-level statistics provide denser, more transferable predictive information than individual SNPs. This enables the gene-level FDRreg models to effectively borrow statistical strength and assign higher prior probabilities of association to shared genes. At the SNP level, where shared signals are much sparser, the model remains more conservative.

Certain methodological caveats regarding statistical assumptions are worth mentioning. SNP, MAGMA, and TWAS statistics exhibited local dependence through LD, gene proximity, and shared expression predictors. Although the clearest theoretical guarantees assume independence, standard FDR procedures are generally robust under positive-regression or weak local dependence, as shown in previous studies
Beyond methodological innovation, our analyses uncovered biologically meaningful discoveries.

Rationale for choosing the FDR regression framework

While several related approaches, such as conditional FDR (condFDR), IHW, and AdaPT, can also leverage external information in significance testing, we chose the FDRreg framework because it is uniquely suited to the specific goals and relatively high
dimensional nature of our study. As described earlier, condFDR typically handles only one related trait. Although extensions to handle additional traits have been proposed

, the method relies on kernel density estimation (KDE), which can perform poorly in sparse regions of the data. It is also more challenging to extend to a high number of covariates, as the algorithm was designed to handle one covariate at one time. While the authors propose an iterative approach, it is assumed that each new round of analysis incorporates genuinely new information (independent of any previous covariates), which may not be practical as many biological annotations or data from related phenotypes are correlated. An iterative procedure also increases the computational burden.
IHW was originally designed to handle a single covariate
stratification; after stratification, a weighted FDR procedure is applied. Given that we have a relatively large number of features, a stratification
based approach may not be the most effective; in addition, IHW requires binning of continuous covariates, which may lead to loss of information.
Similarly, while AdaPT offers modeling flexibility, its sequential discovery process can be
computationally intensive at our scale and offers less direct interpretation of individual covariate effects.

In contrast, as shown in our simulations and applications, FDRreg scales efficiently to up to millions of hypotheses (e.g., millions of SNPs) while handling a large number of covariates (both continuous and categorical). Furthermore, this framework provides a useful layer of mechanistic insight: the estimated regression coefficients directly quantify the direction and magnitude of each covariate’s contribution, revealing which specific traits or biological annotations are most informative for predicting true associations with a given psychiatric disorder. Several limitations and future directions warrant consideration. First, the biological covariates utilized in this study represent a curated, rather than exhaustive, view of psychiatric biology.
Future studies should explore a broader array of functional databases and covariates, such as immune, regulatory, and multi-omic annotations.
Also, the biological annotations require initial construction for each disease domain, though once established, they can be readily incorporated into analyses.

Furthermore, because databases like Open Targets and DAVID are dynamically updated, the exact historical variables used here (extracted in February 2020) cannot be perfectly regenerated via live queries. To ensure reproducibility, we provide the exact frozen annotation matrix used for our model fitting (Table S1.21).

Also, the gene-level covariates represent prioritization choices and may preferentially highlight genes supported by current neurobiology knowledge, potentially under-prioritizing less-studied mechanisms

Second, the majority of GWAS studies are based on European populations, and the results may not be directly generalizable to other ethnicities. On the other hand, the FDRreg framework may be useful to improve the statistical power of GWAS in non-European or minority ethnic groups, as shown in our application to the East Asian GWAS studies of SCZ.

Due to the broad coverage of psychiatric disorders and large number of genes highlighted from this study, we only selected 2 genes from the analysis of ASD for further experimental and mechanistic studies. Further experimental studies are required to elucidate the functional role of other genes uncovered in this study.

Shared signals can nevertheless illuminate general neurodevelopmental mechanisms and support drug repurposing for clinically comorbid conditions. Conversely, disorder-specific loci may be more informative for differential diagnosis and targeted therapeutics development. The balance between these objectives depends partly on covariate choice; future analyses could emphasize mechanism-specific annotations when disorder-enriched discovery is desired. Integration of FDRreg with frameworks designed to pinpoint disorder-specific loci, such as DDx
, represents a promising direction for combining improved discovery power with formal differentiation of related psychiatric disorders.
This study establishes FDRreg as a powerful framework for maximizing discovery
by leveraging pleiotropy and functional annotations.
By identifying hundreds of additional psychiatric risk genes with potential biological relevance, we demonstrate that sophisticated

can extract substantial additional signals from current resources. The strengthened drug-target enrichments suggest important translational applications, while the novel biological pathways provide new hypotheses for psychiatric disorder mechanisms.

As GWAS sample sizes continue to grow and biological annotations become increasingly sophisticated, frameworks like FDRreg will be essential for extracting maximum insight from genetic data to advance our understanding of psychiatric disorders and identify therapeutic opportunities.
